# How to upload a long PDF and get a plain-English summary from Claude

> **In short:** You can drop a PDF directly into a Claude chat and ask for a plain-English summary plus a list of action points. It works on the free plan for normal-sized documents; very long files may need a paid plan.

You've got a 40-page vendor contract, a dense research paper, or a user manual that reads like it was translated by a robot. You don't have time to read all of it. Claude, the AI assistant made by Anthropic, can read the PDF for you and hand back a short summary — and, just as usefully, a list of the bits you'd actually want to act on. This guide walks you through it, start to finish.

## Before you start

- **An Anthropic account.** Free to create at claude.ai. You can sign up with an email address or a Google account.
- **A modern browser** (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari) or the Claude mobile app on iOS or Android. The app and the website work the same way for this task.
- **Your PDF saved on the device** you're using — somewhere you can browse to it (Downloads, Desktop, iCloud, Google Drive). Screen photos of documents also work; we'll cover that.
- **About 10 minutes** for your first try. After that, the same flow takes about two.
- **A quick honesty note:** Claude summarizes what the document says. It does not give legal, medical, or financial advice, and it can occasionally misread a number or a clause. Treat the summary as a fast first pass, not a final verdict.

## Step 1 — Open Claude and start a new chat

Go to claude.ai in your browser, or open the Claude app. If you're not already signed in, enter your email and password, or choose **Continue with Google**. Once you're in, look for a **New chat** button — on the website it's usually at the top-left of the sidebar; on the mobile app it's often a plus sign or a **New conversation** option at the bottom of the chat list. Tap or click it once. A fresh, empty conversation opens, with a message box at the bottom.

**If it looks different:** if you don't see "New chat," look for a **pencil icon**, a **+**, or the words **Start new chat**. On older app versions the button may sit inside a top-right menu (three dots ⋯ or three lines).

💬 Example: nothing to type yet — just open the empty chat so the next step has somewhere to land.

You'll know it worked when you see a blank message box with no previous messages above it.

## Step 2 — Attach your PDF

Click the **paperclip icon** 📎 on the left side of the message box (on the website) or tap the **+** plus button (on the mobile app). A small menu appears with options like **Upload from computer**, **Upload from device**, or simply a list of your recent files. Choose your PDF. The file name appears as a small chip just above the message box, usually with a file-size number next to it.

**If it looks different:** some versions show a button that says **Add files** instead of a paperclip; on older apps the attachment option lives behind a **⋯** three-dot menu. If you only have a printed paper, you can photograph each page with your phone, save the photos as a PDF (most phone gallery apps have a "print to PDF" option), and upload that instead.

💬 Example: choose a file called something like `vendor-contract-2026.pdf` — any PDF you want summarized.

You'll know it worked when a small file chip with the PDF's name shows up under the message box, and the paperclip button briefly highlights or shows a checkmark.

## Step 3 — Ask Claude to summarize it in plain English, plus flag the things you should act on

Click into the message box and type a short instruction telling Claude what you want. Be specific about two things: the **format** (a short summary, plus a list of action points) and the **audience** (you, a non-lawyer reading fast). Press **Enter** (or tap the upward arrow ✉︎ on mobile) to send. The model takes a few seconds to a minute or two — longer PDFs take longer — and then a written reply appears in the chat.

**If it looks different:** some app versions use a small **paper-plane** icon instead of an arrow to send. If the reply is slow, that's normal for big files; don't re-send the message or you'll get two summaries.

💬 Example: *"Read this PDF and give me (1) a 5-sentence plain-English summary, (2) a bulleted list of the 5 most important points I need to know before signing or acting on it, and (3) anything in the document that looks risky, surprising, or unusual. I'm not a lawyer, so keep the language simple."*

You'll know it worked when Claude's reply shows up underneath your message, with a short summary paragraph followed by clearly separated bullet points.

## Step 4 — Ask a follow-up question to test the summary

A summary is only useful if it's accurate. In the same chat (don't start a new one — Claude already has the PDF in mind), type a follow-up question that checks something specific from the document. Then compare Claude's answer against the actual PDF. This is the single most useful habit you can build, and it takes ten seconds.

**If it looks different:** if Claude's answer is vague, ask again with a sharper question — for example, naming the exact page number or section you care about.

💬 Example: *"On page 4, what does the document say about cancellation? In one sentence."* Then open your PDF to page 4 and read the relevant lines yourself.

You'll know it worked when Claude's answer matches what the PDF actually says — or, if it doesn't, you've just caught a misunderstanding before it cost you anything.

## Step 5 — Ask for the summary in a format you can use

Now that the summary is accurate, ask Claude to reshape it for wherever you need it: a short note to your team, a checklist for a meeting, a comparison table, or even a few questions you can ask the other party. This is where the time savings really show up — one document becomes several ready-to-use pieces.

**If it looks different:** if Claude refuses or seems to forget the PDF, scroll up to your original message and click **Copy** on it, then paste the text into a brand-new chat along with your new instruction. Starting fresh sometimes helps when the conversation gets long.

💬 Example: *"Turn the summary into a checklist I can bring to a meeting, with three columns: 'Decision needed', 'Who decides', and 'Deadline'. Keep it under 10 items."*

You'll know it worked when you can copy Claude's output straight into an email, a Notion page, or a meeting agenda without much editing.

## Common mistakes

- **Starting a new chat before uploading the PDF.** A fresh chat has no memory of past conversations, and Claude can't read files you didn't share. Always upload and ask in the same chat.
- **Trusting the summary without checking.** AI assistants sometimes paraphrase a clause in a way that smooths over an important detail. The 10-second check in Step 4 catches this almost every time.
- **Uploading a scanned PDF as images, then expecting it to "just work."** Some scanned PDFs are really just pictures of pages, and Claude may not read them perfectly. If the summary looks confused, try a text-based PDF (the kind you exported from Word, Google Docs, or a real PDF editor) instead.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** the next time you get a long terms-of-service update, a school policy document, or a 30-page apartment lease, you can have a plain-English version of it in your hands in under five minutes — and a list of the few clauses worth actually reading.
- **For your business or work:** vendor contracts, research reports, internal policy PDFs, and user manuals stop being a multi-hour reading job. You get the gist fast, you flag the riskiest items, and you walk into meetings already knowing what's on page 12.
- **If you're just getting started:** start with something low-stakes — a user manual for a gadget you own, or a public research paper from a topic you like. Build the habit of "upload → ask for a 5-sentence summary → check one detail" before you trust it on anything important.

## Try it now

Pick any PDF already on your computer — a manual, a report, anything over 10 pages — and run through Steps 1 to 4 right now. Ten minutes from now, you'll have a summary, a short list of things to act on, and one verified fact. That's the whole skill.
